Welcome to the third edition of the Basic Sciences Quarterly, covering July through September 2026 across our six departments. This issue arrives during Postdoc Appreciation Week (October 12 to 16), so it opens with a section recognizing the accomplishments of postdoctoral scholars in our labs, together with details on our career panel, Pave Your Own Path: What Is Possible After the Postdoc, on Wednesday, October 14. Notable Papers, Faculty in the News, and Funding & Awards also include Q2 items identified after the last issue went to press, marked “added after publication”. Please also save the dates for a December 9 and 10 visit by Jeff Saucerman, Ph.D. (University of Virginia), who will give a seminar and lead a hands-on network modeling workshop. As always, we welcome your feedback.

L. Fernando Santana, Ph.D. & Adriane Joo, Ph.D.
Vice Dean for Basic Sciences & Director of Research Strategy and Innovation for Basic Sciences, UC Davis School of Medicine

December VDBS Events · Dr. Jeff Saucerman: Invited Speaker Seminar & Hybrid Modeling Workshop ▶
Dec 9 & 10
VDBS Event

Invited Speaker Seminar: “Mechanistic Machine Learning of Cardiac Regulatory Networks”

Wed, Dec 9, 2026 · 2:00 to 3:00 PM · GBSF Auditorium

Jeff Saucerman, Ph.D., University of Virginia

Jeff Saucerman, Ph.D., is Professor of Biomedical Engineering and Cardiovascular Medicine at the University of Virginia, where he is a faculty member of the Robert M. Berne Cardiovascular Research Center. His lab combines logic-based network models, machine learning, and high-content imaging to predict how cardiac cells respond to drugs and disease signals, and developed Netflux, an open tool for modeling biological networks. He trained in bioengineering at UC San Diego and was a postdoctoral fellow in cardiac physiology with Donald Bers.

VDBS Event

Hybrid Workshop: How to Model Your Favorite Biological Network with Netflux

Thu, Dec 10, 2026 · 3:00 to 5:00 PM, followed by a reception · GBSF Auditorium

Jeff Saucerman, Ph.D., University of Virginia

Led by Jeff Saucerman. Participants will build a small predictive computational model of a biological network of their choice using Netflux, a free web app. The agenda includes a hands-on introduction, sharing and discussing network schematics, paired work time on your own model, and a group reflection. Please bring a laptop with WiFi and a cartoon image of a signaling pathway you would like to model. A reception follows the workshop.

Workshop FlyerNetflux Web App

12 spotlights

Postdoctoral scholars drive much of the discovery reported in this newsletter. They advance our research, strengthen collaborations, and mentor the students who will follow them. Postdoc Spotlights · Biochemistry & Molecular Medicine

PostdocBiochemistry & Molecular MedicinePublicationInvited Talks

Mohamed Abuelanin

Dennis Lab · Biochemistry & Molecular Medicine

A third-year postdoc, Mohamed developed a sequencing approach that enables affordable and accurate near-complete genome assemblies. He used it to lead a study generating new genomes for prairie and meadow voles, two closely related species with divergent social behaviors, and identified a prairie-vole-specific duplication of a brain-expressed vasopressin receptor gene as a possible contributor to pair bonding.

  • Lead author, Cell Genomics (August 2026), in a special telomere-to-telomere (T2T) issue
  • Selected to present at the Biology of Genomes meeting, Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory (May 2026)
  • Selected to present at the Telomere-to-Telomere Face-to-Face meeting (September 2026)
Cell Genomics paper (PubMed)
PostdocBiochemistry & Molecular MedicineTranslationPublicationMentoring

Sohaib Mahri

Li Lab · Biochemistry & Molecular Medicine
  • Clinical and veterinary translation: advanced the cGMP manufacturing and development of BAQ13-LNP (TR-002), supporting a Phase 1 clinical trial in solid tumors (NCT07189195) and a veterinary trial in dogs with glioblastoma; also advancing Pyro-PBC LNP (TR-003) for photodynamic therapy trials in cats with head and neck cancers.
  • Publications: first author, Biomaterials (2026), on the clinical translation of BAQ13 nanoparticles; co-author of papers in Nano-Micro Letters, Small Science, Frontiers in Immunology, and Nanomedicine (2025).
  • Award: Postdoctoral Travel Award recipient, Summer 2025.
  • Mentoring and outreach: mentored more than 10 students in nanomedicine, experimental design, and translational research; invited speaker for the Sacramento Charter High School Science Outreach Program (2023, 2024); contributed to the UC Davis Comprehensive Cancer Center “Day of Light” public event.

Postdoc Spotlights · Physiology & Membrane Biology

PostdocPhysiology & Membrane BiologyMentoringPublicationInvited Talks

Diego Lopez Mateos

Yarov-Yarovoy Lab · Physiology & Membrane Biology · Center for Precision Medicine and Data Sciences

Diego works at the intersection of biophysics, protein design, and precision medicine. By modeling ion channel conformational landscapes, he studies how individual genetic variants influence channel function and drug response, and applies these insights to design targeted therapeutic modulators, including mini-proteins, antibodies, and macrocycles.

  • Played a leadership role in the 2026 CPMDS Summer Intern Program (July 6 to 31), a four-week immersive research experience for six community college students, developing and delivering lectures and hands-on sessions on protein structure prediction, AlphaFold, neural networks, and how genetic variation shapes treatment response, and guiding the interns through their capstone presentations
  • Mentored undergraduate researcher Frederick Ha in developing computational tools for de novo therapeutic protein design, presented at the 2026 UC Davis Undergraduate Research, Scholarship and Creative Activities Conference
  • First author, “Exploring voltage-gated sodium channel conformations and protein-protein interactions using AlphaFold2,” Journal of General Physiology (2026)
  • Talks on de novo design of ion channel modulators using deep learning at the 2026 Biophysical Society Annual Meeting (San Francisco) and the 2026 SGP-EpIC Symposium at UC Davis
JGP paper (PubMed)

Gonzalo Hernandez-Hernandez

Clancy Lab · Physiology & Membrane Biology · Center for Precision Medicine and Data Sciences

A computational biophysicist and UC Davis Chancellor’s Postdoctoral Fellow, Gonzalo builds mechanistic, multiscale models of how medications and inherited variants influence vascular smooth muscle function, with the goal of more precise antihypertensive therapy and a virtual artery for precision medicine.

  • Selected to present “Modeling Vascular Function Across Scales: From Angiotensin II Receptor Type 1 Signaling to Vessel Function” at Finding Your Inner Modeler, an NSF-sponsored workshop at UC Irvine (August 2026), with a supporting travel grant
  • Co-author, “Large-scale synthetic data enable digital twins of human excitable cells,” eLife (2026)
eLife paper (PubMed)
PostdocPhysiology & Membrane BiologyPublicationsMentoring

Khoa Ngo

Clancy Lab · Physiology & Membrane Biology · Center for Precision Medicine and Data Sciences

Khoa combines structural modeling, molecular simulation, and machine learning to understand how drugs interact with proteins involved in cardiovascular function, and how protein structure and genetic variation shape drug response.

  • First author, “BoltzOmics: Predicting genetic variant effects on drug binding with Boltz-2,” iScience (2026), an open-source platform that uses deep learning and structure prediction to evaluate how variants alter drug binding, assessed on hERG, NaV1.5, HER2, and CYP3A4
  • First author, “CATVariant: a web server for integrated protein variant interpretation,” Nucleic Acids Research (2026)
  • Co-led 2026 CPMDS Summer Intern Program sessions on “Molecules in Motion: Simulating Dynamics of Biomolecules” and “Drug Design in Precision Medicine”

Postdoc Spotlights · Pharmacology

PostdocPharmacologyPublication

Dylan Lanser

Gelli Lab · Pharmacology

Dylan is a co-author of the lab’s Communications Biology study (July 2026), the first to use a human organoid model of the blood-brain barrier to study how the fungal pathogen Cryptococcus neoformans invades the central nervous system. The team found that the fungus enters brain endothelial cells by macropinocytosis, a route that may also be exploited to deliver therapeutics across the barrier. The study was led by Amelia Bennett, Ph.D., who completed her doctorate in the Gelli Lab in April 2026.

Communications Biology paper (PubMed)

Postdoc Spotlights · Public Health Sciences

PostdocPublic Health SciencesPublication

Hilary Colbeth

Whitmer Lab · Public Health Sciences

Hilary is first author of the LifeAfter90 study in The Lancet Healthy Longevity (August 2026), the first effort to examine dementia incidence after age 90 in a highly diverse cohort. Women over 90 had twice the dementia risk of men, and the racial and ethnic disparities seen in younger adults persisted into the tenth decade of life.

Lancet Healthy Longevity paper (PubMed)

Luis Carvajal-Carmona received $1.7 million from the California Initiative to Advance Precision Medicine to partner with a Federally Qualified Health Center and support genetic testing in rural areas.

Press CoveragePublic Health Sciences

UC Davis Health launches effort to advance at-home cervical cancer screening

Julie Dang leads a pilot with Teal Health to integrate at-home HPV self-collection into routine care for patients due or overdue for cervical cancer screening.

UC Davis Health News · Jul 2026 🔗 Read More
Department NewsPublic Health Sciences

UC Davis Public Health Sciences earns seven-year national reaccreditation

The Council on Education for Public Health reaccredited the Public Health Sciences graduate program for seven years, its highest term. Chair Brad Pollock credited the program’s faculty, students, staff, and alumni.

2 items added
Press CoverageMedical Microbiology & Immunology

Regulatory T cells altered in children with autism

Two MIND Institute studies in the Journal of Neuroinflammation, with Paul Ashwood, characterized regulatory T cells in autistic children and tested whether increasing them reduces inflammation and behavioral changes in a model of maternal immune activation.

Press CoverageMedical Microbiology & Immunology

Toxic PCBs, sex-biased genes and the developing brain

Coverage of the Janine LaSalle lab’s Genome Biology study identifying a female placental-brain axis that may protect against prenatal PCB exposure.
